abstract: Summary Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common form of primary liver cancer with poor prognosis. Sorafenib, a first-line treatment for advanced HCC, has shown limited clinical benefits due to the onset of drug resistance. Thus, it is imperative to comprehend the mechanisms underlying sorafenib resistance and explore strategies to overcome or delay it. Here, we established HCC patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models with acquired resistance to sorafenib and performed comprehensive proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses on these models. The active cell cycle pathway along with the active cyclin-dependent kinase CDK1 and DNA-dependent protein kinase PRKDC was identified through KEGG pathway enrichment and kinase substrate enrichment analyses. Upon investigating the potential of combining sorafenib with putative kinase inhibitors, we found that the combination displays synergistic anti-proliferative effects in the sorafenib-resistant liver cancer cell line, thus providing a proof of concept for phosphoproteomic-guided design of precision medicine.

Experimental model and study participant details
Patient samples
This study enrolled a cohort of four patients diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The demographic and clinical characteristics of the patient samples, including age, sex, and disease status, are presented in
Table S1
. Informed consent was obtained from all patients prior to sample collection, and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhongshan Hospital of Fudan University (approval number: B2021-689R). Tumor samples were collected from the enrolled HCC patients to establish PDX models, which were classified as sorafenib-sensitive.
22
Notably, each pair of sorafenib-sensitive and sorafenib-resistant PDX models included in this study was derived from the same patient. The detailed procedures for establishing the PDX models are described in the “
method details
” section.
Cell lines
The Huh7 human HCC cell line was obtained from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). Additionally, the sorafenib-resistant Huh7R cell line was established through long-term exposure to the drug32. Both cell lines were routinely checked for mycoplasma contamination using the MycoBlue Mycoplasma Detector (Vazyme, China). The cell lines were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Hyclone, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 1% penicillin, and 1% streptomycin. Cell morphology images were captured using a Nikon microscope.
Mice
The male BALB/c nude mice were housed in a temperature-controlled, specific pathogen-free environment with a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They were provided with sterile food and water
ad libitum
. The mice were 5 weeks old at the time of tumor implantation and were of wild-type genotype. All animal care and experimental protocols were approved by the Shanghai Medical Experimental Animal Care Commission.
Method details
Establishment of sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX models
The limited availability of tumor specimens from sorafenib-resistant HCC patients presents a substantial obstacle to study of drug resistance mechanisms.
19
Our previous study demonstrated that HCC PDX models closely mirror the genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic characteristics of the original tumor.
22
This correlation enhances our understanding of clinical responses and patient heterogeneity and provides a valuable platform for evaluating novel treatments. According to the methodology outlined in previous work,
22
each
in situ
model was randomly divided into two groups of male mice: ① control group (n=6); ② sorafenib group (n=6). Upon reaching a tumor volume of 50 mm³, the experimental group was administered sorafenib daily at a dose of 30 mg/kg. After 28 days, the mice were euthanized, and the length (a) and width (b) of the tumors were measured. The tumor volume was calculated using the formula V=1/2ab
2
. The inhibitory effect of sorafenib on tumor growth was assessed using the Tumor Growth Inhibition index (TGI = ΔT/ΔC (%), where T = tumor volume of the experimental group, C = tumor volume of the control group). Models with TGI values ranging between 0-20% were classified as sorafenib-sensitive. The obtained four sorafenib-sensitive models were further divided into groups and medicated. The model with the median tumor volume in each experimental group was continuously passed to the next generation until TGI exceeded 100%, indicating the successful development of an HCC PDX model that had acquired resistance to sorafenib. Thus, we successfully developed four sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX models for this investigation.
Tissue lysis and protein extraction
The tumor tissues were prepared for analysis by cutting them into pieces using surgical scissors and transferring them to grinding tubes. The tubes were frozen in liquid nitrogen and pulverized using the SKXL frozen grinding apparatus (Biheng, Shanghai, China) at 2,500 rpm and -30°C for 45 seconds. The resulting fine powder was lysed in urea lysis buffer at a tissue-to-buffer ratio of 1:10 (v/v). The lysis buffer consisted of 8 M urea, 75 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris (pH 8.0), 1 mM EDTA, and 1:100 (v/v) Halt™ Protease & Phosphatase Single-Use Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 78442). The lysate was vortexed for 60 seconds and subsequently incubated on ice for 10 minutes to ensure sufficient lysis. The lysate was centrifuged at 18,000 g for 10 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was transferred to a new tube. The protein concentration was estimated using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225) following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Peptide digestion and desalting
One milligram of protein from each sample was adjusted to a final concentration of 6 mg/mL using lysis buffer. The protein was first reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for one hour at 37°C and then alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide for 45 minutes at room temperature in the dark. Subsequently, the samples were diluted 1:3 with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and subjected to proteolytic digestion with LysC (Wako Chemicals, Japan) at a 1:200 enzyme-to-substrate ratio for four hours at 25°C. Mass spectrometry-grade trypsin (Promega, USA) was then added to the solution at a 1:50 enzyme-to-substrate ratio and incubated overnight at 25°C. To quench the trypsin digestion, the samples were acidified to a pH of around 2.5 by adding 10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). The resulting tryptic digests were centrifuged at 1,500 g for 10 minutes to remove insoluble materials, and the supernatant containing the peptides was transferred to new tubes. The peptides were desalted using reversed-phase C18 solid-phase extraction (SPE) columns (Waters, Milford, CT) with 0.1% TFA for loading and washing and 0.1% TFA/50% acetonitrile (ACN) for elution. The desalted peptides were dried using a lyophilizer (Christ, Germany) and stored at -80°C.
iTRAQ labeling
The peptides were labeled with iTRAQ 8-plex reagents (AB Sciex, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. Specifically, 400 μg of lyophilized peptides were dissolved in 80 μL of 0.5 M triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer. Subsequently, the iTRAQ 8-plex reagents were dissolved in 200 μL of isopropanol and transferred to the eight sample tubes. Each sample mixture was vortexed and incubated at room temperature for 2 hours, then concentrated to 50 μL using a vacuum concentrator. Finally, the samples labeled with the eight isotopomeric iTRAQ reagents were combined and evaporated to dryness.
Peptide fractionation by basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography (bRPLC)
To improve the depth of identification, basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography (bRPLC) was used to fractionate the peptides.
24
Peptide separation was performed using basic-pH RP solvent A (5 mM NH
4
COOH, 2% acetonitrile, adjusted to pH 10.0 with 25% NH
3
·H
2
O) and a non-linear gradient of basic-pH RP solvent B (5 mM ammonium formate, 90% acetonitrile, adjusted to pH 10.0 with 25% NH
3
·H
2
O). A total of 3.2 mg of iTRAQ 8-plex labeled peptides was reconstituted in 950 μL solvent A and loaded onto a Waters XBridge peptide BEH300 C18 column (4.6 mm × 250 mm, OD 3.5 μm) at a flow rate of 1 mL/min using an Acquity UPLC H-Class Bio system (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). For peptide elution, a 90-minute gradient was set with the following specifications: 0% solvent B (9 minutes), 6% solvent B (4 minutes), 6% to 28.5% solvent B (50 minutes), 28.5% to 34% solvent B (5.5 minutes), 34% to 60% solvent B (13 minutes), and a hold at 60% solvent B for 8.5 minutes. The eluted fractions were collected every minute from 3 to 91 minutes in a serpentine fashion. The collected fractions were then pooled into 24 fractions, with a 6% of each fraction reserved for global proteomic analysis. The remaining 94% of the fractions were combined into 13 fractions for subsequent phosphopeptide enrichment and phosphoproteome analysis.
Enrichment of phosphopeptides by Fe-NTA
Phosphopeptide enrichment was performed using a commercial High-Select™ Fe-NTA Phosphopeptide Enrichment Kit (Thermo Scientific, A32992) following the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. The lyophilized peptide fractions were reconstituted in 200 μL of loading buffer (80% ACN, 0.1% TFA), and one spin column in the kit was divided into seven equal parts. Each fraction was mixed with one of these parts and incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes. The peptide-resin mixture was then transferred to a filter tip (Axygen, TF-20-L-R-S), and the supernatant was removed after centrifugation. The resins, which had adsorbed phosphopeptides, were sequentially washed three times with 200 μL of washing buffer (80% ACN, 0.1% TFA) and three times with 200 μL of water to remove unbound peptides. To release the phosphopeptides from the resins, 50 μL of elution buffer (50% ACN, 5% NH
3
·H
2
O) was added twice. All centrifugation steps were conducted at 200 × g. The eluates were collected and dried using vacuum concentrator for subsequent mass spectrometry analysis.
Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis
Global proteome and phosphoproteome fractions were analyzed using the same instrumentation. LC-TIMS-MS/MS analysis was performed using a nanoElute nanoflow ultrahigh pressure LC system (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany) coupled to the timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics), equipped with a CaptiveSpray nanoelectrospray ion source (Bruker Daltonics). Peptide samples were dissolved in solvent A (0.1% formic acid), and 200 ng of peptide digest was loaded onto a capillary C18 column (25 cm length, 75 μm inner diameter, 1.6 μm particle size, 120 Å pore size; IonOpticks, Fitzroy, VIC, Australia). Solvent B, which is an acetonitrile solution containing 0.1% formic acid, was employed. For global proteomics, peptides were separated at 50°C using a 90-minute gradient at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The 2–22% solvent B gradient was applied for 70 minutes, followed by a 22–37% solvent B step from 70 to 80 minutes, a 37–80% solvent B step from 80 to 82 minutes, and an additional 8-minute wash at 80% solvent B. The total runtime for each analysis was 90 minutes.
For phosphoproteomics, the gradient involved a stepwise progression of solvent B from 2–22% for 90 minutes, followed by a transition to 22–37% solvent B from 90 to 100 minutes, and then another transition to 37–80% solvent B from 100 to 110 minutes, with a subsequent 10-minute wash at 80% solvent B. The total runtime for each analysis was 120 minutes. Data acquisition was performed using the timsTOF Pro in parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode.
51
,
52
Data-dependent acquisition was performed using 10 PASEF MS/MS scans for each survey scan. TIMS stepping was used to analyze the iTRAQ-labeled peptides. This involved subjecting each precursor to fragmentation twice using specific parameters. The collision energy increased linearly as a function of mobility, ranging from 1/k0 = 0.6 V·s/cm
2
to 1.6 V·s/cm
2
. The first step utilized a collision energy range of 44.8-89.6 eV, while the second step utilized a range of 32-64 eV. The mass spectrometer resolution was 38,000 at m/z = 1222. Ions with a charge state of 2-5 and a m/z between 100 and 1,700 were specifically chosen for fragmentation if their intensity exceeded 5,000. Masses below 700 m/z were isolated using a window of 2 Th, while masses above 800 m/z were isolated using a window of 3 Th. For masses between 700 and 800 m/z, the isolation widths were extrapolated from values within the range of 2-3 Th. Peptide loading was normalized to the total ion chromatograms obtained from 200 ng injections of HeLa whole cell lysate standard (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Peptide and protein identification
The MS raw files were searched against combined human and mouse reference databases proteome
21
(Uniprot FASTA file, downloaded on 08/20/2020) supplemented with common contaminants using PEAKS Online.
53
The precursor and fragment mass error tolerances were set to 15 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Trypsin was specified as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to 3 missed cleavage sites. For all searches, fixed modifications were set as carbamidomethylation of cysteine, iTRAQ 8-plex at lysine, and the N-terminal residue. Variable modifications included oxidation of methionine (M), N-terminal protein acetylation, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, and, for phosphoproteome data, phosphorylation on serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues. The false discovery rate (FDR) of peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) and protein groups was set at 1% for filtering based on the target-decoy strategy. Peptide length was set to range from 7 to 45 amino acids. The Ascore provided by the Peaks Online software reflects the confidence in the localization of identified phosphorylation sites. In this study, a threshold of Ascore > 20 was applied to filter the phosphopeptide data.
54
A total of 17,096 proteins and 67,586 phosphosites were identified. Missing values were imputed with the minimum value across our proteome and phosphoproteome data. To correct sample loading differences, proteome and phosphosite data were subjected to quantile normalization (
https://wkomics.omicsolution.com/wkomics/main/
).
Targeted parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) analysis
The targeted Parallel Reaction Monitoring (PRM) analysis was conducted using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer coupled with an LC system (EvoSep One, EvoSep Inc., Odense, Denmark). For this analysis, commercially synthesized phosphorylated peptides, TQEGS(+79.97)LSAR of PRKDC (S2624) phosphoprotein, and VYT(+79.97)HEVVTLWYR of CDK1 (T161) phosphoprotein, were used. Peptide separation was performed at a flow rate of 300 nL/min using a mobile phase consisting of 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and an acetonitrile solution with 0.1% formic acid (solvent B). Peptide separation was conducted on a 50 cm analytical column (Acclaim PepMapTM RSLC, 75 μm x 50 cm, nanoViper™ C18, 2 μm, 100 Å) using the following gradient: 0–46 minutes, 2–25% B; 46–56 minutes, 25–55% B; 56–57 minutes, 55–95% B; 58–65 minutes, 95% B. The MS1 scan range was set to 300–1800 m/z with a resolution of 60,000. The data acquisition parameters included a dynamic gain control (AGC) target value of 5 × 10
4
, an m/z isolation window of 2, and a normalized HCD collision energy of 33%. A library was constructed using Skyline (v.4.2) based on the data collected using the previously employed data-dependent acquisition (DDA) method. All RAW files collected during the PRM analysis were imported into Skyline for matching and processing, and the product ion peak areas were extracted for quantification.
Bioinformatics analysis
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was utilized to calculate p-values in this study. Proteins or phosphorylation sites exhibiting a fold change greater than 1.25 or less than 0.8, along with p-values less than 0.05, were considered statistically significant.
55
,
56
Hypothesis testing, volcano plots, Spearman correlation analysis of samples, and partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) were conducted for proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets using a web-based platform (
https://wkomics.omicsolution.com/wkomics/main/
).
Pathway analysis
The Metascape web-based platform (RRID:
SCR_016620
) was employed to analyze Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment using our differentially expressed proteins. Pathview (
https://pathview.uncc.edu/
),
27
an online tool, was utilized to visualize KEGG pathway maps and annotate them by filling phosphoprotein nodes with colors representing the log2 ratio of normalized phosphoprotein abundance in the resistant group compared to the control. Specifically, red, grey, and green colors were used to indicate higher, similar, and lower abundance of phosphoproteins in the resistant group compared to the control, respectively.
Kinase activity prediction
Kinase-substrate enrichment analysis (KSEA) was utilized to assess changes in kinase activity
29
by examining significantly differentiated phosphosites in the resistant group compared to the matched control group. KSEA was performed using the ‘KSEAapp’ R package (version 1.0). Known kinase-substrate relationships from the PhosphoSitePlus (PSP)
57
and NetworKIN 3.0
58
databases were employed in our analysis. A kinase score was assigned based on the collective phosphorylation status of its substrates, which was then transformed into a z-score. The threshold for significantly enriched kinases was set at p < 0.05 and a substrate count of ≥ 5. To eliminate the effect of protein expression, we normalized the quantified phosphosites by dividing the intensity value of the corresponding protein for each sample. For proteins with multiple phosphosites, each site was treated independently. The normalized p-sites were also used for KSEA using the same methodology. The dysregulated kinases were highlighted on the kinome map, which was constructed using the KinMap tool (
http://www.kinhub.org/kinmap/index.html
).
Western blot analysis
In this study, tumor tissue proteins were extracted using the urea buffer method, and protein quantification was performed using a BCA kit. Subsequently, 5× sample loading buffer was added by volume and the lysate was boiled for 10 minutes at 99°C. Protein blotting analysis was performed by separating the boiled samples using SDS-PAGE and transferring them to a nitrocellulose membrane (Millipore). The membranes were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin for 1 hour at room temperature, washed with TBST, and then incubated overnight at 4°C with a specific primary antibody. The primary antibodies used were recombinant Anti-DNA PKcs (phospho S2056) antibody (RRID:
AB_11001004
), Anti-DNA PKcs antibody, Anti-CDK1 (phospho T161) antibody (RRID:
AB_2260040
), Anti-CDK1 antibody (RRID:
AB_11155333
), Anti-Rb antibody (RRID:
AB_2848193
), Anti-Rb (phospho T373) antibody (RRID:
AB_2177344
), Anti-Vimentin antibody (RRID:
AB_10562134
), Anti-Vimentin (phospho S56) antibody from Abcam, and antibody β-Actin Rabbit mAb (RRID:
AB_2768234
) from ABclonal. The membranes were washed three times with TBST at room temperature and incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature. Following three washes, the membranes were incubated with ECL luminescent solution, and data were collected using a chemiluminescent imager (Bio-Rad). The densitometric quantification of the target protein bands was assessed using ImageJ software and expressed as target/β-Actin ratios.
Drugs
Sorafenib, Ro-3306 (a CDK1 inhibitor), and KU-57788 (a PRKDC inhibitor) were purchased from MedChemExpress Co., Ltd. for
in vivo
pharmacologic studies.
Cell proliferation and IC
50
assays
For the cell proliferation assay, Huh7 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1,500 cells per well and cultured for 24 hours prior to treatment. The data are presented as relative viability values for the treatment group compared to the control group. Relative cell growth was determined daily and normalized to day 0. For the IC
50
assay, 4,000 Huh7 cells were plated per well in a 96-well plate and treated with various doses of sorafenib for 72 hours. Cell viability was assessed at different time points using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8, Dojindo, Japan), following the manufacturer’s instructions. Each assay was repeated independently at least three times. All data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9 software (RRID:
SCR_002798
).
Long-term clonogenic assays
Huh7 cells were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 10
4
cells per well and treated with the indicated kinase inhibitors for 10–12 days. The culture medium was changed twice a week to maintain cell viability. The cells were observed using an optical microscope (Olympus, Japan) and fixed with 4% formaldehyde in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 30 minutes. The cells were stained with 0.1% crystal violet (Solarbio, Beijing, China) diluted in water for 15 minutes and images were taken using an Epson Scanner (Seiko Epson Corporation, Nagano-Ken, Japan). Cell confluence in each well was quantified using ImageJ software (version 1.53; RRID:
SCR_003070
).
Combination effect analysis
The combination indices (CIs) of Ro-3306/KU-57788 and sorafenib were evaluated as described previously with the CompuSyn software (CompuSyn Inc.) based on the Chou–Talalay theory.

CI < 1, CI = 1, and CI > 1 represent synergistic, additive, and antagonistic effects, respectively.

The lysate was vortexed for 60 seconds and subsequently incubated on ice for 10 minutes to ensure sufficient lysis. The lysate was centrifuged at 18,000 g for 10 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was transferred to a new tube. The protein concentration was estimated using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225) following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Peptide digestion and desalting
One milligram of protein from each sample was adjusted to a final concentration of 6 mg/mL using lysis buffer. The protein was first reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for one hour at 37°C and then alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide for 45 minutes at room temperature in the dark. Subsequently, the samples were diluted 1:3 with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and subjected to proteolytic digestion with LysC (Wako Chemicals, Japan) at a 1:200 enzyme-to-substrate ratio for four hours at 25°C. Mass spectrometry-grade trypsin (Promega, USA) was then added to the solution at a 1:50 enzyme-to-substrate ratio and incubated overnight at 25°C. To quench the trypsin digestion, the samples were acidified to a pH of around 2.5 by adding 10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). The resulting tryptic digests were centrifuged at 1,500 g for 10 minutes to remove insoluble materials, and the supernatant containing the peptides was transferred to new tubes. The peptides were desalted using reversed-phase C18 solid-phase extraction (SPE) columns (Waters, Milford, CT) with 0.1% TFA for loading and washing and 0.1% TFA/50% acetonitrile (ACN) for elution. The desalted peptides were dried using a lyophilizer (Christ, Germany) and stored at -80°C.
iTRAQ labeling
The peptides were labeled with iTRAQ 8-plex reagents (AB Sciex, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. Specifically, 400 μg of lyophilized peptides were dissolved in 80 μL of 0.5 M triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer. Subsequently, the iTRAQ 8-plex reagents were dissolved in 200 μL of isopropanol and transferred to the eight sample tubes. Each sample mixture was vortexed and incubated at room temperature for 2 hours, then concentrated to 50 μL using a vacuum concentrator. Finally, the samples labeled with the eight isotopomeric iTRAQ reagents were combined and evaporated to dryness.
Peptide fractionation by basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography (bRPLC)
To improve the depth of identification, basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography (bRPLC) was used to fractionate the peptides.
24
Peptide separation was performed using basic-pH RP solvent A (5 mM NH
4
COOH, 2% acetonitrile, adjusted to pH 10.0 with 25% NH
3
·H
2
O) and a non-linear gradient of basic-pH RP solvent B (5 mM ammonium formate, 90% acetonitrile, adjusted to pH 10.0 with 25% NH
3
·H
2
O). A total of 3.2 mg of iTRAQ 8-plex labeled peptides was reconstituted in 950 μL solvent A and loaded onto a Waters XBridge peptide BEH300 C18 column (4.6 mm × 250 mm, OD 3.5 μm) at a flow rate of 1 mL/min using an Acquity UPLC H-Class Bio system (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). For peptide elution, a 90-minute gradient was set with the following specifications: 0% solvent B (9 minutes), 6% solvent B (4 minutes), 6% to 28.5% solvent B (50 minutes), 28.5% to 34% solvent B (5.5 minutes), 34% to 60% solvent B (13 minutes), and a hold at 60% solvent B for 8.5 minutes. The eluted fractions were collected every minute from 3 to 91 minutes in a serpentine fashion. The collected fractions were then pooled into 24 fractions, with a 6% of each fraction reserved for global proteomic analysis. The remaining 94% of the fractions were combined into 13 fractions for subsequent phosphopeptide enrichment and phosphoproteome analysis.
Enrichment of phosphopeptides by Fe-NTA
Phosphopeptide enrichment was performed using a commercial High-Select™ Fe-NTA Phosphopeptide Enrichment Kit (Thermo Scientific, A32992) following the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. The lyophilized peptide fractions were reconstituted in 200 μL of loading buffer (80% ACN, 0.1% TFA), and one spin column in the kit was divided into seven equal parts. Each fraction was mixed with one of these parts and incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes. The peptide-resin mixture was then transferred to a filter tip (Axygen, TF-20-L-R-S), and the supernatant was removed after centrifugation. The resins, which had adsorbed phosphopeptides, were sequentially washed three times with 200 μL of washing buffer (80% ACN, 0.1% TFA) and three times with 200 μL of water to remove unbound peptides. To release the phosphopeptides from the resins, 50 μL of elution buffer (50% ACN, 5% NH
3
·H
2
O) was added twice. All centrifugation steps were conducted at 200 × g. The eluates were collected and dried using vacuum concentrator for subsequent mass spectrometry analysis.
Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis
Global proteome and phosphoproteome fractions were analyzed using the same instrumentation. LC-TIMS-MS/MS analysis was performed using a nanoElute nanoflow ultrahigh pressure LC system (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany) coupled to the timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics), equipped with a CaptiveSpray nanoelectrospray ion source (Bruker Daltonics). Peptide samples were dissolved in solvent A (0.1% formic acid), and 200 ng of peptide digest was loaded onto a capillary C18 column (25 cm length, 75 μm inner diameter, 1.6 μm particle size, 120 Å pore size; IonOpticks, Fitzroy, VIC, Australia). Solvent B, which is an acetonitrile solution containing 0.1% formic acid, was employed. For global proteomics, peptides were separated at 50°C using a 90-minute gradient at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The 2–22% solvent B gradient was applied for 70 minutes, followed by a 22–37% solvent B step from 70 to 80 minutes, a 37–80% solvent B step from 80 to 82 minutes, and an additional 8-minute wash at 80% solvent B. The total runtime for each analysis was 90 minutes.
For phosphoproteomics, the gradient involved a stepwise progression of solvent B from 2–22% for 90 minutes, followed by a transition to 22–37% solvent B from 90 to 100 minutes, and then another transition to 37–80% solvent B from 100 to 110 minutes, with a subsequent 10-minute wash at 80% solvent B. The total runtime for each analysis was 120 minutes. Data acquisition was performed using the timsTOF Pro in parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode.
51
,
52
Data-dependent acquisition was performed using 10 PASEF MS/MS scans for each survey scan. TIMS stepping was used to analyze the iTRAQ-labeled peptides. This involved subjecting each precursor to fragmentation twice using specific parameters. The collision energy increased linearly as a function of mobility, ranging from 1/k0 = 0.6 V·s/cm
2
to 1.6 V·s/cm
2
. The first step utilized a collision energy range of 44.8-89.6 eV, while the second step utilized a range of 32-64 eV. The mass spectrometer resolution was 38,000 at m/z = 1222. Ions with a charge state of 2-5 and a m/z between 100 and 1,700 were specifically chosen for fragmentation if their intensity exceeded 5,000. Masses below 700 m/z were isolated using a window of 2 Th, while masses above 800 m/z were isolated using a window of 3 Th. For masses between 700 and 800 m/z, the isolation widths were extrapolated from values within the range of 2-3 Th. Peptide loading was normalized to the total ion chromatograms obtained from 200 ng injections of HeLa whole cell lysate standard (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Peptide and protein identification
The MS raw files were searched against combined human and mouse reference databases proteome
21
(Uniprot FASTA file, downloaded on 08/20/2020) supplemented with common contaminants using PEAKS Online.
53
The precursor and fragment mass error tolerances were set to 15 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Trypsin was specified as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to 3 missed cleavage sites. For all searches, fixed modifications were set as carbamidomethylation of cysteine, iTRAQ 8-plex at lysine, and the N-terminal residue. Variable modifications included oxidation of methionine (M), N-terminal protein acetylation, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, and, for phosphoproteome data, phosphorylation on serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues. The false discovery rate (FDR) of peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) and protein groups was set at 1% for filtering based on the target-decoy strategy. Peptide length was set to range from 7 to 45 amino acids. The Ascore provided by the Peaks Online software reflects the confidence in the localization of identified phosphorylation sites. In this study, a threshold of Ascore > 20 was applied to filter the phosphopeptide data.
54
A total of 17,096 proteins and 67,586 phosphosites were identified. Missing values were imputed with the minimum value across our proteome and phosphoproteome data. To correct sample loading differences, proteome and phosphosite data were subjected to quantile normalization (
https://wkomics.omicsolution.com/wkomics/main/
).
Targeted parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) analysis
The targeted Parallel Reaction Monitoring (PRM) analysis was conducted using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer coupled with an LC system (EvoSep One, EvoSep Inc., Odense, Denmark). For this analysis, commercially synthesized phosphorylated peptides, TQEGS(+79.97)LSAR of PRKDC (S2624) phosphoprotein, and VYT(+79.97)HEVVTLWYR of CDK1 (T161) phosphoprotein, were used. Peptide separation was performed at a flow rate of 300 nL/min using a mobile phase consisting of 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and an acetonitrile solution with 0.1% formic acid (solvent B). Peptide separation was conducted on a 50 cm analytical column (Acclaim PepMapTM RSLC, 75 μm x 50 cm, nanoViper™ C18, 2 μm, 100 Å) using the following gradient: 0–46 minutes, 2–25% B; 46–56 minutes, 25–55% B; 56–57 minutes, 55–95% B; 58–65 minutes, 95% B. The MS1 scan range was set to 300–1800 m/z with a resolution of 60,000. The data acquisition parameters included a dynamic gain control (AGC) target value of 5 × 10
4
, an m/z isolation window of 2, and a normalized HCD collision energy of 33%. A library was constructed using Skyline (v.4.2) based on the data collected using the previously employed data-dependent acquisition (DDA) method. All RAW files collected during the PRM analysis were imported into Skyline for matching and processing, and the product ion peak areas were extracted for quantification.
Bioinformatics analysis
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was utilized to calculate p-values in this study. Proteins or phosphorylation sites exhibiting a fold change greater than 1.25 or less than 0.8, along with p-values less than 0.05, were considered statistically significant.
55
,
56
Hypothesis testing, volcano plots, Spearman correlation analysis of samples, and partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) were conducted for proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets using a web-based platform (
https://wkomics.omicsolution.com/wkomics/main/
).
Pathway analysis
The Metascape web-based platform (RRID:
SCR_016620
) was employed to analyze Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment using our differentially expressed proteins. Pathview (
https://pathview.uncc.edu/
),
27
an online tool, was utilized to visualize KEGG pathway maps and annotate them by filling phosphoprotein nodes with colors representing the log2 ratio of normalized phosphoprotein abundance in the resistant group compared to the control. Specifically, red, grey, and green colors were used to indicate higher, similar, and lower abundance of phosphoproteins in the resistant group compared to the control, respectively.
Kinase activity prediction
Kinase-substrate enrichment analysis (KSEA) was utilized to assess changes in kinase activity
29
by examining significantly differentiated phosphosites in the resistant group compared to the matched control group. KSEA was performed using the ‘KSEAapp’ R package (version 1.0). Known kinase-substrate relationships from the PhosphoSitePlus (PSP)
57
and NetworKIN 3.0
58
databases were employed in our analysis. A kinase score was assigned based on the collective phosphorylation status of its substrates, which was then transformed into a z-score. The threshold for significantly enriched kinases was set at p < 0.05 and a substrate count of ≥ 5. To eliminate the effect of protein expression, we normalized the quantified phosphosites by dividing the intensity value of the corresponding protein for each sample. For proteins with multiple phosphosites, each site was treated independently. The normalized p-sites were also used for KSEA using the same methodology. The dysregulated kinases were highlighted on the kinome map, which was constructed using the KinMap tool (
http://www.kinhub.org/kinmap/index.html
).
Western blot analysis
In this study, tumor tissue proteins were extracted using the urea buffer method, and protein quantification was performed using a BCA kit. Subsequently, 5× sample loading buffer was added by volume and the lysate was boiled for 10 minutes at 99°C. Protein blotting analysis was performed by separating the boiled samples using SDS-PAGE and transferring them to a nitrocellulose membrane (Millipore). The membranes were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin for 1 hour at room temperature, washed with TBST, and then incubated overnight at 4°C with a specific primary antibody. The primary antibodies used were recombinant Anti-DNA PKcs (phospho S2056) antibody (RRID:
AB_11001004
), Anti-DNA PKcs antibody, Anti-CDK1 (phospho T161) antibody (RRID:
AB_2260040
), Anti-CDK1 antibody (RRID:
AB_11155333
), Anti-Rb antibody (RRID:
AB_2848193
), Anti-Rb (phospho T373) antibody (RRID:
AB_2177344
), Anti-Vimentin antibody (RRID:
AB_10562134
), Anti-Vimentin (phospho S56) antibody from Abcam, and antibody β-Actin Rabbit mAb (RRID:
AB_2768234
) from ABclonal. The membranes were washed three times with TBST at room temperature and incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature. Following three washes, the membranes were incubated with ECL luminescent solution, and data were collected using a chemiluminescent imager (Bio-Rad). The densitometric quantification of the target protein bands was assessed using ImageJ software and expressed as target/β-Actin ratios.
Drugs
Sorafenib, Ro-3306 (a CDK1 inhibitor), and KU-57788 (a PRKDC inhibitor) were purchased from MedChemExpress Co., Ltd. for
in vivo
pharmacologic studies.
Cell proliferation and IC
50
assays
For the cell proliferation assay, Huh7 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1,500 cells per well and cultured for 24 hours prior to treatment. The data are presented as relative viability values for the treatment group compared to the control group. Relative cell growth was determined daily and normalized to day 0. For the IC
50
assay, 4,000 Huh7 cells were plated per well in a 96-well plate and treated with various doses of sorafenib for 72 hours. Cell viability was assessed at different time points using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8, Dojindo, Japan), following the manufacturer’s instructions. Each assay was repeated independently at least three times. All data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9 software (RRID:
SCR_002798
).
Long-term clonogenic assays
Huh7 cells were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 10
4
cells per well and treated with the indicated kinase inhibitors for 10–12 days. The culture medium was changed twice a week to maintain cell viability. The cells were observed using an optical microscope (Olympus, Japan) and fixed with 4% formaldehyde in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 30 minutes. The cells were stained with 0.1% crystal violet (Solarbio, Beijing, China) diluted in water for 15 minutes and images were taken using an Epson Scanner (Seiko Epson Corporation, Nagano-Ken, Japan). Cell confluence in each well was quantified using ImageJ software (version 1.53; RRID:
SCR_003070
).
Combination effect analysis
The combination indices (CIs) of Ro-3306/KU-57788 and sorafenib were evaluated as described previously with the CompuSyn software (CompuSyn Inc.) based on the Chou–Talalay theory.
59
CI < 1, CI = 1, and CI > 1 represent synergistic, additive, and antagonistic effects, respectively.
In vivo
validation of combination therapy in sorafenib resistant HCC PDXs
Briefly, sorafenib-resistant HCC sample from a patient was trimmed and cut into approximately 20 mm
3
fragments. These fragments were then implanted subcutaneously in the right flanks of anesthetized 5-week-old male BALB/c nude mice within 3 hours. Once the tumor volume reached around 150 mm
3
, and mice were randomly assigned to four groups. The treatment groups consisted of vehicle, Sorafenib (30 mg/kg/day, oral gavage), KU-57788 (4 mg/kg/day, intraperitoneal injection), or a combination of these drugs at the same dose and schedule as single-agent dosing. Tumor volume was measured twice a week. Mouse weight, ascites formation, and survival rates were monitored throughout the treatment process. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test.

Introduction
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common type of liver cancer, is projected to reach 1 million new cases by 2025.
1
Despite the increasing utilization of surgical and locoregional therapies globally estimates indicate that approximately 50%–60% of HCC patients ultimately require systemic treatments.
2
Targeted therapies have created an encouraging trend in the management of advanced HCC.
3
Sorafenib, a molecular targeted therapeutic agent, was the first drug approved for unresectable HCC by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). However, its clinical efficacy was unsatisfactory, with a short improvement in survival time (about 3–6 months), and acquired drug resistance typically develops within six months of treatment initiation.
4
,
5
,
6
Understanding the mechanisms of drug resistance is crucial for developing effective strategies to improve therapeutic outcomes in HCC. Ongoing trials are investigating combination therapies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors,
5
tyrosine kinase inhibitors,
7
and even combinations of two immunotherapy regimens.
2
Phosphorylation, an essential post-translational modification found in at least 75% of the proteome,
8
is regulated by protein kinases. This modification impacts various cellular processes, including cell cycle progression and signaling.
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
Dysregulation of signaling networks often leads to diseases, rendering protein kinases prime drug targets.
13
There are over 73 small molecule inhibitors approved by the FDA, and 175 compounds are undergoing clinical trials.
14
These targeted inhibitors typically reduce the activity of known oncogenic signaling pathways, but comprehending their therapeutic mechanisms extends beyond genetic and protein levels.
14
The advancement of liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) has facilitated the identification and quantification of sample-specific proteins in a high-throughput manner. Recently, quantitative proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses have helped identify intrinsic cancer signaling networks and their activated kinases in a variety of cancers, such as HCC,
15
glioblastoma,
16
T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia,
17
and urothelial carcinoma.
18
To date, only one study has utilized tumor tissues from sorafenib-treated HCC patients.
19
This study employed proteomics and phosphoproteomics analyses on biopsied tissues from HCC patients before and during sorafenib treatment, revealing a wide range of signaling pathways involved in tumor progression and drug resistance. However, the limited availability of non-renewable biopsy material poses a challenge to obtaining sustainable large-scale proteomic data. Given the scarcity of clinically resistant patient samples, patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models have played an increasingly pivotal role in clinical research.
20
In the PDX model, the human stroma is replaced by host murine components, but human tumor proteins can be predominantly distinguished from murine stromal proteins through the identification of species-specific peptide sequences.
21
These models retain the key characteristics of the primary tumor, including histology, genome, transcriptome, proteome, and phosphoproteome,
20
,
22
making them a reliable option for preclinical studies. Moreover, phosphoproteomics analyses of PDX models have revealed potential tumor suppressors, mechanisms of drug resistance, novel targets, and successful multidrug combination regimens in various diseases.
16
,
21
,
23
Our previous study has successfully established the sorafenib-resistant PDX models.
22
Here, we further utilized a multiplex iTRAQ MS-based proteomics approach to comprehensively quantify the proteome and phosphoproteome of four paired sorafenib-resistant and sorafenib-sensitive PDX models. KEGG enrichment analysis and kinase substrate enrichment analysis (KSEA) identified CDK1 and PRKDC kinases in the cell cycle pathway as potential targets for overcoming sorafenib resistance in HCC. We then evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of combining sorafenib with Ro-3306 (a CDK1 inhibitor) or KU-57788 (a PRKDC inhibitor) against sorafenib-resistant HCC using both cell lines and PDX models. Both combination therapies were found to be synergistic in overcoming drug resistance. This study provides critical insights into the mechanisms of tumor progression and resistance to cancer therapy, emphasizing the valuable role of PDX models in identifying and validating potential biomarkers and signaling pathways for enhancing cancer treatment.
Results
Workflow of quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics analysis
The scarcity of tumor specimens from sorafenib-resistant HCC patients poses a significant challenge in studying drug resistance mechanisms. To comprehensively understand the development of acquired sorafenib resistance in patients with advanced HCC, we conducted quantitative proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses of four pairs of sorafenib-sensitive/resistant PDX tumors. The schematic workflow is presented in
Figure 1
. Tumor tissue samples were subjected to protein extraction using 8M urea buffer, followed by protein reduction, alkylation, and tandem Lys-C/trypsin digestion to generate peptides. The resulting peptides were labeled with 8-plex iTRAQ reagents and fractionated using basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography with a non-continuous pooling strategy.
24
A total of 96 fractions was collected and then combined into 24 fractions, which consisted of early, intermediate, and late eluting fractions.
24
,
25
Of these 24 fractions, 6% were used for global proteomics, whereas the remaining 94% were combined into 13 fractions that were enriched for phosphopeptides using immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography. The obtained peptides were subsequently analyzed using LC-MS/MS with a timsTOF Pro instrument. Three technical replicates were performed for each fraction to ensure analytical accuracy and reliability.

The comprehensive iTRAQ-based global proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis identified 17,096 proteins and 67,586 peptides, including 50,593 phosphopeptides. Of these, 9,366 proteins (with an average of 8,200 per sample) and 33,621 phosphopeptides matched the human proteome (

Furthermore, paired samples exhibited higher correlation coefficients than unpaired samples, indicating molecular heterogeneity in PDX tumor tissues. Supervised partial least squares discriminant analysis highlighted that proteomic and phosphoproteomic levels could differentiate between paired drug-resistant and control tumor samples (

Pathway enrichment analysis reveals dysregulated cell cycle pathway in sorafenib-resistant tumor
This study identified 2,120 phosphorylation sites that were significantly altered, with 944 upregulated and 1,176 downregulated in resistant tissues (Wilcoxon signed-rank test,
p
< 0.05, fold change 1.25,

26
to identify KEGG pathways associated with the differentially expressed phosphosites. The resulting top 20 pathways were visually represented in the heatmap (
Figure 3
B). Furthermore, utilizing Metascape enrichment network visualization, we illustrated intra- and inter-cluster similarities of enriched terms and predicted interactions among biological pathways (

In contrast, sorafenib-sensitive tumors exhibited enrichment of pathways involved in cell communication, endocrine system function, and energy metabolism, which are essential for normal liver function. These pathways encompassed tight junction, adherens junction, insulin signaling pathway, thyroid hormone signaling pathway, vascular smooth muscle contraction, endocytosis, and glucagon signaling pathway. These results suggest a higher degree of tumor malignancy in the drug-resistant group. Similarly, the proteome exhibited comparable results to the phosphoproteome (Wilcoxon signed-rank test,
p
< 0.05, fold change 1.25,
Figures S5
A and S5B). The notable enrichment of cell cycle signaling pathways in both the proteomic and phosphoproteomic data of drug-resistant tumor tissues prompted us to map differentially expressed phosphoproteins to the KEGG cell cycle pathway using Pathview
27
(
Figure 3
C). The network analysis highlighted several upregulated key node proteins in drug-resistant tumors. This observation indicates that the cell cycle pathway is highly active in drug-resistant tumors, suggesting a strong tumor proliferative capacity.

Identification of dysregulated kinases associated with cell cycle signaling pathway in sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX models
Protein kinases have emerged as important drug targets over the past two decades, primarily due to their frequent dysregulation in various diseases.
28
Sorafenib, a potent multikinase inhibitor drug, is closely associated with phosphorylation.
19
To infer changes in kinase activity in drug-resistant tumors, we subjected the differentially expressed phosphosites as substrates to KSEA.
29
The KSEA results indicated that several kinases, including cell cycle-dependent kinases 1/2/4 (CDK1/2/4), ATM, PRKDC, AURKA/B, ATR, NEK2, HIPK2 MAK, PLK1/4, and TTK, showed higher activity in drug-resistant tumors, whereas the kinase activity of PRKG1 and SGK1 was increased in the sorafenib-sensitive tumor group (
Figures 4
A and 4B). By mapping these kinases to the human kinome tree, we discovered significant dysregulation in the CMGC, AGC, and atypical PIKK protein kinase families (
Figure S4
B). KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that enriched kinases were mainly associated with the cell cycle signaling pathway (
Figure S4
C), implying that the onset of sorafenib resistance in HCC could be due to the activation of the cell cycle pathway. These kinases, including ATM, ATR, and PRKDC, play key roles in DNA repair. Cells have evolved an intricate DNA repair mechanism to limit DNA damage progression by triggering cell cycle checkpoints and repairing DNA damage before it interferes with the replication process. In some tumor cells, enhanced DNA repair capacity after replication and genotoxic stress has been observed, leading to accumulated genomic damage and ultimately cell death.

Discussion
HCC is an aggressive and malignant form of adenocarcinoma.
35
However, there is a limited availability of effective therapies for addressing sorafenib resistance in advanced HCC. Our research specifically addressed the crucial issue of discovering potential therapeutic strategies for overcoming acquired resistance to sorafenib in HCC through comprehensive profiling of proteomics and phosphoproteomics of sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX mouse models. To our knowledge, this study represented the first quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis of tumors from sorafenib-resistant PDX models, providing valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of acquired sorafenib resistance in patients with advanced HCC. The analyses revealed detailed changes in the proteome and phosphoproteome between sorafenib-resistant and sorafenib-sensitive PDX tumors, leading to the identification of a significant number of altered proteins and phosphosites. Further exploration of the enriched pathways uncovered significant activation of the cell cycle signaling pathway in sorafenib-resistant tumors, suggesting its potential role as a compensatory pathway driving tumor progression. In contrast, sorafenib-sensitive tumors exhibited enriched pathways associated with cell communication, endocrine system function, and energy metabolism. These differences may indicate distinct underlying mechanisms between sorafenib-resistant and sorafenib-sensitive tumors and could potentially account for the variation in clinical responses observed in HCC patients.
Nowadays, six systemic therapies have gained FDA approval for HCC based on phase III clinical trials, including atezolizumab plus bevacizumab,
36
sorafenib,
6
lenvatinib,
37
regorafenib,
38
cabozantinib,
39
and ramucirumab.
40
Notably, five of these therapies target protein kinases, highlighting the importance of protein kinase-dependent signaling networks in the progression of HCC. Transitioning our focus onto the role of kinases, this research has identified the dysregulation of several key players, including CDK1/2/4, ATM, PRKDC, and AURKA/B, among others. The significant modifications we have observed in phosphorylation sites, along with the variety of kinases identified through KSEA, illustrate the multidimensional nature of sorafenib resistance. The elevated activity of these kinases suggests their potential roles in driving the resistance process. Notably, CDK1 and PRKDC were identified as potential kinases in this study, suggesting that inhibitors targeting these kinases could represent novel therapeutic options for drug-resistant HCC.
CDK1 is recognized as an oncogenic protein due to its regulation of the G2/M cell cycle checkpoint, which allows for cell progression through mitosis. CDK1 is commonly overexpressed or exhibits enhanced kinase activity in various cancers, including lung cancer,
41
HCC,
15
,
42
and urothelial carcinoma of the bladder.
18
Targeting CDK1 has shown promise in improving cancer treatment outcomes. For example, studies have demonstrated that inhibition of CDK1 using Ro-3306 increases the efficacy of sorafenib treatment for HCC.
42
The inhibition of CDK1 is under investigation as a potential therapeutic approach for several other cancers, such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
43
,
44
PRKDC, also known as DNA-dependent protein kinase, is a core kinase that repairs non-homologous end joining DNA damage. Its high expression is often associated with a poor prognosis in various cancers, including HCC
45
,
46
and breast cancer.
47
In many cancers, the upregulation of DNA repair activity leads to drug resistance, suggesting that PRKDC could be a potential target for overcoming resistance.
48
,
49
The discrepancy observed between the
in vitro
and
in vivo
findings can be attributed to several key factors. First, the notable differences between the
in vitro
and
in vivo
environments, such as the complex tumor microenvironment and systemic factors present in the PDX models, may lead to divergent drug responses compared with the simplified
in vitro
conditions.
20
Second, the inherent tumor heterogeneity within the PDX models represents a significant challenge.
20
The presence of diverse subpopulations of cancer cells, each potentially relying on different signaling pathways for survival, could hinder the ability of the combination therapy to elicit a synergistic effect. Furthermore, the study may have been limited in its capacity to fully optimize the drug administration regimen to overcome sorafenib resistance.
23
The complex interplay between the tumor, its microenvironment, and the pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics of the drugs requires a more in-depth investigation to unravel the specific mechanisms underlying the observed discrepancy.
In summary, the results of KEGG enrichment analysis and KSEA revealed the activation of the cell cycle pathway in sorafenib-resistant tumors, along with enhanced activity of the associated kinases CDK1 and PRKDC. Based on these findings, the two kinase inhibitors were administered with sorafenib in sorafenib-resistant cell line and mice, respectively. The drug combinations exhibited synergistic inhibition of proliferation at the cellular level. These findings have the potential to be translated into clinical applications, enabling precision therapy and more effective treatment for patients. Furthermore, this approach can be extended to investigate resistance patterns in other cancer types and their response to different drugs. By doing so, we can advance our knowledge of carcinogenesis and cancer drug resistance on a broader scale, contributing to the development of more effective treatment strategies.
Limitations of the study
The sample size in this study was limited. To validate the efficacy of the combination therapies, it is crucial to include a larger cohort of sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX models, considering the heterogeneity of patients. Additionally, we point out here that the detailed mechanism of how kinases function in sorafenib-resistant HCC remains to be explored in future studies.

The Huh7 human HCC cell line was obtained from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). Method details
Establishment of sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX models
The limited availability of tumor specimens from sorafenib-resistant HCC patients presents a substantial obstacle to study of drug resistance mechanisms.
19
Our previous study demonstrated that HCC PDX models closely mirror the genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic characteristics of the original tumor.
22
This correlation enhances our understanding of clinical responses and patient heterogeneity and provides a valuable platform for evaluating novel treatments. According to the methodology outlined in previous work,
22
each
in situ
model was randomly divided into two groups of male mice: ① control group (n=6); ② sorafenib group (n=6). Upon reaching a tumor volume of 50 mm³, the experimental group was administered sorafenib daily at a dose of 30 mg/kg. After 28 days, the mice were euthanized, and the length (a) and width (b) of the tumors were measured. The tumor volume was calculated using the formula V=1/2ab
2
. The inhibitory effect of sorafenib on tumor growth was assessed using the Tumor Growth Inhibition index (TGI = ΔT/ΔC (%), where T = tumor volume of the experimental group, C = tumor volume of the control group). Models with TGI values ranging between 0-20% were classified as sorafenib-sensitive. The obtained four sorafenib-sensitive models were further divided into groups and medicated. The model with the median tumor volume in each experimental group was continuously passed to the next generation until TGI exceeded 100%, indicating the successful development of an HCC PDX model that had acquired resistance to sorafenib. Thus, we successfully developed four sorafenib-resistant HCC PDX models for this investigation.
Tissue lysis and protein extraction
The tumor tissues were prepared for analysis by cutting them into pieces using surgical scissors and transferring them to grinding tubes. The tubes were frozen in liquid nitrogen and pulverized using the SKXL frozen grinding apparatus (Biheng, Shanghai, China) at 2,500 rpm and -30°C for 45 seconds. The resulting fine powder was lysed in urea lysis buffer at a tissue-to-buffer ratio of 1:10 (v/v). The lysis buffer consisted of 8 M urea, 75 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris (pH 8.0), 1 mM EDTA, and 1:100 (v/v) Halt™ Protease & Phosphatase Single-Use Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 78442). The lysate was vortexed for 60 seconds and subsequently incubated on ice for 10 minutes to ensure sufficient lysis. The lysate was centrifuged at 18,000 g for 10 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was transferred to a new tube. The protein concentration was estimated using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225) following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Peptide digestion and desalting
One milligram of protein from each sample was adjusted to a final concentration of 6 mg/mL using lysis buffer. The protein was first reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for one hour at 37°C and then alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide for 45 minutes at room temperature in the dark. Subsequently, the samples were diluted 1:3 with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and subjected to proteolytic digestion with LysC (Wako Chemicals, Japan) at a 1:200 enzyme-to-substrate ratio for four hours at 25°C. Mass spectrometry-grade trypsin (Promega, USA) was then added to the solution at a 1:50 enzyme-to-substrate ratio and incubated overnight at 25°C. To quench the trypsin digestion, the samples were acidified to a pH of around 2.5 by adding 10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). The resulting tryptic digests were centrifuged at 1,500 g for 10 minutes to remove insoluble materials, and the supernatant containing the peptides was transferred to new tubes. The peptides were desalted using reversed-phase C18 solid-phase extraction (SPE) columns (Waters, Milford, CT) with 0.1% TFA for loading and washing and 0.1% TFA/50% acetonitrile (ACN) for elution. The desalted peptides were dried using a lyophilizer (Christ, Germany) and stored at -80°C.
iTRAQ labeling
The peptides were labeled with iTRAQ 8-plex reagents (AB Sciex, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. Specifically, 400 μg of lyophilized peptides were dissolved in 80 μL of 0.5 M triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer. Subsequently, the iTRAQ 8-plex reagents were dissolved in 200 μL of isopropanol and transferred to the eight sample tubes. Each sample mixture was vortexed and incubated at room temperature for 2 hours, then concentrated to 50 μL using a vacuum concentrator. Finally, the samples labeled with the eight isotopomeric iTRAQ reagents were combined and evaporated to dryness.
Peptide fractionation by basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography (bRPLC)
To improve the depth of identification, basic pH reversed-phase liquid chromatography (bRPLC) was used to fractionate the peptides.
24
Peptide separation was performed using basic-pH RP solvent A (5 mM NH
4
COOH, 2% acetonitrile, adjusted to pH 10.0 with 25% NH
3
·H
2
O) and a non-linear gradient of basic-pH RP solvent B (5 mM ammonium formate, 90% acetonitrile, adjusted to pH 10.0 with 25% NH
3
·H
2
O). A total of 3.2 mg of iTRAQ 8-plex labeled peptides was reconstituted in 950 μL solvent A and loaded onto a Waters XBridge peptide BEH300 C18 column (4.6 mm × 250 mm, OD 3.5 μm) at a flow rate of 1 mL/min using an Acquity UPLC H-Class Bio system (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). For peptide elution, a 90-minute gradient was set with the following specifications: 0% solvent B (9 minutes), 6% solvent B (4 minutes), 6% to 28.5% solvent B (50 minutes), 28.5% to 34% solvent B (5.5 minutes), 34% to 60% solvent B (13 minutes), and a hold at 60% solvent B for 8.5 minutes. The eluted fractions were collected every minute from 3 to 91 minutes in a serpentine fashion. The collected fractions were then pooled into 24 fractions, with a 6% of each fraction reserved for global proteomic analysis. The remaining 94% of the fractions were combined into 13 fractions for subsequent phosphopeptide enrichment and phosphoproteome analysis.
Enrichment of phosphopeptides by Fe-NTA
Phosphopeptide enrichment was performed using a commercial High-Select™ Fe-NTA Phosphopeptide Enrichment Kit (Thermo Scientific, A32992) following the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. The lyophilized peptide fractions were reconstituted in 200 μL of loading buffer (80% ACN, 0.1% TFA), and one spin column in the kit was divided into seven equal parts. Each fraction was mixed with one of these parts and incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes. The peptide-resin mixture was then transferred to a filter tip (Axygen, TF-20-L-R-S), and the supernatant was removed after centrifugation. The resins, which had adsorbed phosphopeptides, were sequentially washed three times with 200 μL of washing buffer (80% ACN, 0.1% TFA) and three times with 200 μL of water to remove unbound peptides. To release the phosphopeptides from the resins, 50 μL of elution buffer (50% ACN, 5% NH
3
·H
2
O) was added twice. All centrifugation steps were conducted at 200 × g. The eluates were collected and dried using vacuum concentrator for subsequent mass spectrometry analysis.
Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis
Global proteome and phosphoproteome fractions were analyzed using the same instrumentation. LC-TIMS-MS/MS analysis was performed using a nanoElute nanoflow ultrahigh pressure LC system (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany) coupled to the timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics), equipped with a CaptiveSpray nanoelectrospray ion source (Bruker Daltonics). Peptide samples were dissolved in solvent A (0.1% formic acid), and 200 ng of peptide digest was loaded onto a capillary C18 column (25 cm length, 75 μm inner diameter, 1.6 μm particle size, 120 Å pore size; IonOpticks, Fitzroy, VIC, Australia). Solvent B, which is an acetonitrile solution containing 0.1% formic acid, was employed. For global proteomics, peptides were separated at 50°C using a 90-minute gradient at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The 2–22% solvent B gradient was applied for 70 minutes, followed by a 22–37% solvent B step from 70 to 80 minutes, a 37–80% solvent B step from 80 to 82 minutes, and an additional 8-minute wash at 80% solvent B. The total runtime for each analysis was 90 minutes.
For phosphoproteomics, the gradient involved a stepwise progression of solvent B from 2–22% for 90 minutes, followed by a transition to 22–37% solvent B from 90 to 100 minutes, and then another transition to 37–80% solvent B from 100 to 110 minutes, with a subsequent 10-minute wash at 80% solvent B. The total runtime for each analysis was 120 minutes. Data acquisition was performed using the timsTOF Pro in parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode.
51
,
52
Data-dependent acquisition was performed using 10 PASEF MS/MS scans for each survey scan. TIMS stepping was used to analyze the iTRAQ-labeled peptides. This involved subjecting each precursor to fragmentation twice using specific parameters. The collision energy increased linearly as a function of mobility, ranging from 1/k0 = 0.6 V·s/cm
2
to 1.6 V·s/cm
2
. The first step utilized a collision energy range of 44.8-89.6 eV, while the second step utilized a range of 32-64 eV. The mass spectrometer resolution was 38,000 at m/z = 1222. Ions with a charge state of 2-5 and a m/z between 100 and 1,700 were specifically chosen for fragmentation if their intensity exceeded 5,000. Masses below 700 m/z were isolated using a window of 2 Th, while masses above 800 m/z were isolated using a window of 3 Th. For masses between 700 and 800 m/z, the isolation widths were extrapolated from values within the range of 2-3 Th. Peptide loading was normalized to the total ion chromatograms obtained from 200 ng injections of HeLa whole cell lysate standard (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Peptide and protein identification
The MS raw files were searched against combined human and mouse reference databases proteome
21
(Uniprot FASTA file, downloaded on 08/20/2020) supplemented with common contaminants using PEAKS Online.

The precursor and fragment mass error tolerances were set to 15 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Trypsin was specified as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to 3 missed cleavage sites. For all searches, fixed modifications were set as carbamidomethylation of cysteine, iTRAQ 8-plex at lysine, and the N-terminal residue. Targeted parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) analysis
The targeted Parallel Reaction Monitoring (PRM) analysis was conducted using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer coupled with an LC system (EvoSep One, EvoSep Inc., Odense, Denmark). For this analysis, commercially synthesized phosphorylated peptides, TQEGS(+79.97)LSAR of PRKDC (S2624) phosphoprotein, and VYT(+79.97)HEVVTLWYR of CDK1 (T161) phosphoprotein, were used. Peptide separation was performed at a flow rate of 300 nL/min using a mobile phase consisting of 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and an acetonitrile solution with 0.1% formic acid (solvent B). Peptide separation was conducted on a 50 cm analytical column (Acclaim PepMapTM RSLC, 75 μm x 50 cm, nanoViper™ C18, 2 μm, 100 Å) using the following gradient: 0–46 minutes, 2–25% B; 46–56 minutes, 25–55% B; 56–57 minutes, 55–95% B; 58–65 minutes, 95% B. The MS1 scan range was set to 300–1800 m/z with a resolution of 60,000. The data acquisition parameters included a dynamic gain control (AGC) target value of 5 × 10
4
, an m/z isolation window of 2, and a normalized HCD collision energy of 33%. A library was constructed using Skyline (v.4.2) based on the data collected using the previously employed data-dependent acquisition (DDA) method. All RAW files collected during the PRM analysis were imported into Skyline for matching and processing, and the product ion peak areas were extracted for quantification.

Kinase activity prediction
Kinase-substrate enrichment analysis (KSEA) was utilized to assess changes in kinase activity
29
by examining significantly differentiated phosphosites in the resistant group compared to the matched control group. KSEA was performed using the ‘KSEAapp’ R package (version 1.0). Known kinase-substrate relationships from the PhosphoSitePlus (PSP)

The threshold for significantly enriched kinases was set at p < 0.05 and a substrate count of ≥ 5. To eliminate the effect of protein expression, we normalized the quantified phosphosites by dividing the intensity value of the corresponding protein for each sample. For proteins with multiple phosphosites, each site was treated independently. The normalized p-sites were also used for KSEA using the same methodology.
